newsitem.title: UK: Corporates to bear brunt of UK budget tax rises.
newsitem.headline: Corporates to bear brunt of UK budget tax rises.

text.p: Companies, not consumers, look set to bear the brunt of tax rises in Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget on July 2 as the new government attempts to balance election promises with economic management.
Economic theory suggests Brown should hit the personal sector which is already showing signs of overheating as building society windfall payments add to already rising wages.
But election promises mean the government is unlikely to raise income or even value-added tax (VAT), and personal tax allowances also look safe.

"One of the outstanding messages from the election is that parties which break faith on tax are not forgiven. That lesson will not be lost on Tony Blair," said Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch.
"There aren't many ways of getting at the personal sector that Labour hasn't ruled out or hinted are out of bounds, so it looks like the corporate sector will pick up the bill."
Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS, agreed the chancellor's sights are set on companies.

"Recent press leaks suggest politics has defeated economics and there is a significant risk Brown will deliver a package of measures directing a fiscal tightening towards the corporate sector, not the personal."

Privatised utilities already know they face a one-off windfall tax on past "excess" profits, although they still do not know how big the bill will be. But many other companies may also be hit by higher taxes.
UK corporation tax is low by international standards at 33 percent and raising it would be the easiest way to tap the sector. Each one-percentage-point increase would raise around 750 million.
But tax experts said the government is eager to retain overseas business here, and attract new enterprises, so this is not on the cards.

"The UK wants to keep attracting business and the worldwide trend in corporation tax is down, so that suggests no change in the corporate tax rate," said Ian Barlow, head of tax at KPMG, a leading accountancy firm.

A more likely target is the tax credit on companies' dividend payments. This encourages the holding of equities by giving a tax credit to shareholders of 20 percent on dividend payments, representing the tax the company has already paid.

Axing this credit could be presented as a move to encourage companies to retain more profit for investment and would raise five billion stg. Whittling it down by half would raise two or three billion pounds.
But the government's election pledges do not mean the personal sector is totally immune from tax rises, and home-owners are on the front line.
Mortgage interest tax relief (MIRAS) offers a tax break on interest on the first 30,000 pounds of a home loan. Abolishing it would raise around 2.5 billion pounds for the Treasury.
But this measure would hit the most depressed parts of the housing market hardest, so some economists now see stamp duty as a more likely target.
At one percent of the value of purchased property, UK stamp duty is among the lowest in Europe.

"Doubling stamp duty on house purchases would raise half a billion pounds," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets. "And it would need to be introduced immediately to avoid a spike in housing activity."
Households in line for a generous inheritance may find themselves less well off than they hoped.

Barlow at KPMG forecast inheritance tax will be higher on July 2 than its current 40 percent. "The government may also examine the rule whereby gifts can avoid the tax if the giver lives for seven years after the gift is made."
